item.title: Medicine Overview
item.description:
What happened & why it matters

  • Black Death (1348)
    • At the time — medicine utterly helpless

  • Germ Theory (1861)
    • At the time — transformed understanding of disease
    • Long term — enabled vaccines, antibiotics, and modern medicine
  • NHS (1948)
    • At the time — radical state intervention in healthcare
    • Long term — transformed life expectancy and access to medicine

item.title: Religion and medical progress (16-mark)
item.description:
16-mark question · How far do you agree · AO1/AO2

The question

Religion was the main reason why medical knowledge did not improve during the Middle Ages. How far do you agree? (16 marks)

Model answer — Level 4

I strongly agree that religion was the main reason why medical knowledge did not improve during the Middle Ages. This is because the power of the Church meant that ideas which went against religious teaching were not accepted, which limited progress. However, other factors such as lack of technology and government involvement also prevented medical development during this period.

item.title: Anaesthetics (8-mark)
item.description:
8-mark question · Significance · AO1/AO2

The question

Explain the significance of anaesthetics in the development of medicine. (8 marks)

Compare the levels below — same question, different grades. Notice what the higher-level answer does that the lower one doesn’t.

Model answer — Level 4

In the 19th century anaesthetics were significant because even though they allowed surgeons to do more complex surgeries, they still brought new problems. This was because Simpson discovered how effective chloroform was in 1847, surgeons did not understand about infection. This meant that many patients had operations which infected them and they died from blood poisoning or hospital sickness. Chloroform also lead to deaths because surgeons did not understand how powerful it was, like when Hannah Greener died in 1848 for an operation to remove her toenail, which led to opposition against anaesthetics by people who thought they were more harm than good.

item.title: Black Death and Cholera (8-mark)
item.description:
8-mark question · Compare: similarities · AO1/AO2

The question

Compare the Black Death in the Middle Ages with the cholera epidemics in the 19th century. In what ways were they similar? (8 marks)

Compare the levels below — same question, different grades. Notice what the higher-level answer does that the lower one doesn’t.

Model answer — Level 4

The cities in both the 19th Century cholera epidemic and Medieval Black Death were extremely dirty. This dirt was the prime cause of both epidemics – dirty water being the cause of cholera and dirty streets attracting the rats that were infested with Black Death carrying fleas. However, with both diseases people didn’t know the true cause (not until John Snow made the link between cholera and dirty water). Instead for both diseases they believed in causes such as miasmas and God punishing people. This caused thousands of people to die in both epidemics.

item.title: Louis Pasteur (8-mark)
item.description:
8-mark question · Significance · AO1/AO2

The question

Explain the significance of the work of Louis Pasteur for the development of medicine. (8 marks)

Compare the levels below — same question, different grades. Notice what the higher-level answer does that the lower one doesn’t.

Model answer — Level 4

One way in which the work of Louis Pasteur was significant to the development of medicine was that his work changed medical beliefs. For instance, during the Middle Ages, people believed that disease was caused by miasma theory. However, Louis Pasteur discovered that germs caused disease. For example, he discovered Germ Theory which was the idea that microorganisms cause disease, and is still believed to this day. This discovery was significant as it changed the development of medicine by inspiring many scientists who came after Pasteur to discover disease which were proved by experimentation, like Germ Theory.

item.title: Vaccination (8-mark)
item.description:
8-mark question · Source utility · AO3a/AO3b

The question

Compare the levels below — same question, different grades. Notice what the higher-level answer does that the lower one doesn’t.

Model answer — Level 4

Source A shows society’s negative reaction to Edward Jenner’s discovery of the Smallpox vaccination. The cows sprouting from people’s bodies are a representation of the unnatural effects people believed they would develop if they got vaccinated. This is useful because it is a reminder that although the discovery is significant today, it was rejected by a lot of people around the time it was found. The origin of this source states that it was drawn in 1802 by James Gillray only three years after Jenner’s discovery. As the vaccination was still relatively new in 1802 many people did not trust it, especially as Jenner had no way of explaining the effects of his work as germs had yet to be discovered. item.title: BPSF - Medicine Stands Still
item.description:
What happened & why it matters

  • Church adopts Galen (medieval period)
    • At the time — gave authority to medical ideas
    • Long term — prevented new ideas from being accepted
  • Fall of Rome (476 AD)
    • At the time — loss of Roman public health systems
    • Long term — towns became dirtier; disease spread more easily

Key knowledge — DSTEP

Type Item Why it matters
Date c.200 AD Galen writes — his ideas then dominate for the next 1,400 years
Date 476 AD Fall of Rome — loss of Roman public health infrastructure; regression in practical medicine
Date c.1000–1350 Height of medieval medicine — Galenic theory unchanged; Church controls learning
Stat ~1,400 years Galen’s ideas went largely unchallenged (c.200 AD to c.1600 AD)
Stat ~90% Medieval hospitals were Church-run — religion, not science, shaped medical care
Term Four Humours Blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile — the dominant explanation of disease
Term Miasma theory Bad air causes disease — wrong, but not challenged in this period
Term Bloodletting Removing blood to rebalance the humours — harmful treatment used for centuries
Term Church authority The Church backed Galen — questioning him meant questioning God
Person Galen c.200 AD — his dominance is what “standing still” means; wrong in many areas but untouchable
Person Medieval Church Controlled universities and medicine — reinforced Galen as unquestionable authority

Think like a historian

  • What conditions are needed for a wrong idea to stay dominant for 1,400 years?
  • What does it tell us about the relationship between religious authority and scientific progress that Galen’s errors survived until someone was brave enough to dissect a human body?

item.title: BPSF - Beginnings of Change
item.description:
What happened & why it matters

  • Printing press (c.1440)
    • At the time — allowed books to spread fast
    • Long term — new medical ideas could reach a European audience
  • Vesalius publishes (1543)
    • At the time — challenged Galen’s anatomy
    • Long term — transformed how doctors understood the body
  • Harvey’s circulation (1628)
    • At the time — overturned Galen’s blood theory
    • Long term — showed experiment could defeat authority

Key knowledge — DSTEP

Type Item Why it matters
Date c.1440 Gutenberg’s printing press — transformed the spread of ideas across Europe
Date 1453 Fall of Constantinople — Greek scholars fled west, bringing ancient texts
Date 1543 Vesalius publishes De Humani Corporis Fabrica — corrected over 200 Galenic errors
Date 1628 Harvey proves blood circulates — challenged Galen; showed experiment over authority
Stat 200+ Errors in Galen’s anatomy corrected by Vesalius — based on actual human dissection
Stat 20 million Books in circulation within 50 years of the printing press — speed of knowledge spread
Term Renaissance “Rebirth” of classical learning — questioning of authority; new attitudes to knowledge
Term Printing press Gutenberg c.1440 — enabled rapid spread of new ideas across Europe
Term Humanism Renaissance philosophy — humans, not just God, can investigate and understand the world
Term Scientific method Observe, experiment, conclude — the new approach replacing Galen’s authority
Person Vesalius 1543 — overturned Galen through dissection; did not explain why things worked, but what they look like
Person William Harvey 1628 — proved blood circulates; used measurement and experiment
Person Ambroise Paré Renaissance surgeon — improved wound treatment through observation and trial

Think like a historian

  • What is the relationship between communication technology and the pace of intellectual change?
  • If the Renaissance was about new ideas — were the ideas actually new, or was it the speed at which they could now spread that was new?

item.description:
What happened & why it matters

  • Pasteur’s Germ Theory (1861)
    • At the time — explained how disease spreads
    • Long term — enabled vaccines, antibiotics, antiseptics
  • Lister’s antiseptics (1865)
    • At the time — dramatically cut surgical deaths
    • Long term — made complex surgery survivable

Key knowledge — DSTEP

Type Item Why it matters
Date 1796 Jenner — smallpox vaccination; first successful vaccine
Date 1847 Simpson — chloroform anaesthetic; allowed longer, more complex surgery
Date 1861 Pasteur — Germ Theory published; the key breakthrough
Date 1865 Lister — carbolic acid antiseptic; dramatically cut surgical death rates
Date 1882 Koch identifies TB bacterium — Germ Theory put to use
Stat ~50% Operations ended in death from infection before antiseptics
Stat 15% Death rate after surgery dropped to ~15% after Lister’s antiseptics
Stat 400,000+ Europeans dying of smallpox per year before Jenner
Term Germ Theory Disease caused by microbes — Pasteur 1861; foundation of modern medicine
Term Anaesthetic Substance allowing painless surgery — chloroform (Simpson 1847)
Term Antiseptic Kills bacteria to prevent infection — carbolic acid (Lister 1865)
Term Vaccination Using a weakened form of a disease to build immunity
Person Louis Pasteur 1861 — Germ Theory; the single most important breakthrough in this period
Person Robert Koch Identified specific bacteria causing specific diseases — turned theory into practice
Person Joseph Lister Applied Germ Theory to surgery — antiseptic technique
Person James Simpson Chloroform anaesthetic 1847 — removed pain; enabled more complex operations

  • Why is understanding the cause of something so important before you can systematically treat it?
  • Why did it take until 1861 — when microscopes had existed since the 1600s — for Germ Theory to be established?

What happened & why it matters

  • Penicillin (1928–43)

  • NHS (1948)

    • Long term — transformed British life expectancy and access to medicine

    • At the time — revealed the structure of life
    • Long term — enabled genetic engineering, gene therapy, personalised medicine

Type Item Why it matters

Date 1928 Fleming discovers penicillin — the antibiotic revolution begins
Date 1942 Beveridge Report — blueprint for the welfare state
Date 1948 NHS founded — universal free healthcare
Date 1953 Watson and Crick — DNA double helix; foundation of genetic medicine

item.title: Importance of Hippocrates
item.description:
What happened & why it matters

  • Hippocratic Corpus compiled (~400 BC)
    • At the time — first rational framework for medicine
    • Long term — adopted by Galen, then the Church; dominated for 1,400 years

Key knowledge — DSTEP

Type Item Why it matters
Date c.460 BC Hippocrates born — shifted medicine from supernatural to natural explanations
Date c.400 BC Hippocratic Corpus compiled — ~60 texts; the foundation of Western medical theory
Date c.200 AD Galen builds on Hippocrates — extended his ideas; kept them dominant for centuries more
Stat ~60 Hippocratic texts that survived — a library of clinical observation
Stat ~400 Treatments recorded in the Hippocratic Corpus
Term Four Humours Blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile — Hippocratic theory of disease; balance = health
Term Clinical observation Watching and recording symptoms — Hippocrates’ key method; still used today
Term Hippocratic Oath Code of medical ethics — doctors still swear a version today
Term Natural causes Disease caused by nature, not gods — the central breakthrough of Hippocratic medicine
Person Hippocrates ~460 BC — “Father of Medicine”; natural causes; clinical observation; Hippocratic Oath
Person Galen c.200 AD — extended Hippocratic ideas; Four Humours survived through his influence

Think like a historian

  • Why does the shift from supernatural to natural explanations matter so much for medicine — and for science in general?
  • If Hippocrates got the Four Humours completely wrong, why do we still call him the Father of Medicine?

item.title: The Importance of Galen and Doctor Training
item.description:
What happened & why it matters

  • Galen’s pig experiment
    • At the time — demonstrated the brain controls speech
    • Long term — made Galen’s methods seem credible; reinforced his authority
  • Church adopts Galen (medieval period)
    • At the time — stabilised medical education
    • Long term — prevented challenge to Galen for centuries
  • Vesalius corrects Galen (1543)
    • At the time — shocking overturning of authority
    • Long term — opened the door to scientific anatomy

Key knowledge — DSTEP

Type Item Why it matters
Date c.460 BC Hippocrates — natural causes; Galen builds on these foundations
Date c.200 AD Galen active — writes anatomy and medical theory based on animal dissection
Date 1543 Vesalius — exposes Galen’s anatomical errors; begins the overturning of his authority
Date 1876 Koch identifies anthrax — Germ Theory finally displaces Galenic humour theory
Stat 200+ Errors in Galen’s anatomy (based on animal dissection, not human)
Stat ~1,400 years Galen’s ideas dominated medicine after the fall of Rome until the Renaissance
Term Vivisection Dissection of living animals — Galen’s method; led to anatomical errors
Term Four Humours Galen’s extension of Hippocrates — blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile
Term Pig experiment Galen cut vocal cords of a live pig to show the brain controls the voice — impressive but also shows limits of animal work
Term Church authority The Church endorsed Galen — questioning him was near-heresy
Person Hippocrates Foundation for Galen — his natural causes and Four Humours framework
Person Galen c.200 AD — extended Hippocrates; Church adopted his work; wrong about anatomy but right to use observation
Person Vesalius 1543 — showed Galen wrong through human dissection; key challenge to authority
Person Robert Koch 1876 — Germ Theory finally replaced humour theory as the explanation of disease

Think like a historian

  • What’s the difference between following an authority’s method and following their conclusions — and why does that distinction matter?
  • Is Galen’s legacy for medicine ultimately positive or negative, given that his method was revolutionary but his authority prevented progress?

item.title: Impact of the Christian Church on Medicine in the Middle Ages
item.description:
What happened & why it matters

  • Church adopts Galen (medieval)
    • At the time — gave stability to medical education
    • Long term — prevented anatomical progress for centuries
  • Council of Clermont (1130)
    • At the time — banned clergy from surgery
    • Long term — separated surgery from learned medicine; barber-surgeons emerged

Key knowledge — DSTEP

Type Item Why it matters
Date 476 AD Fall of Rome — Church becomes the dominant institution in Western Europe
Date 1130 Council of Clermont — Church restricted clergy from performing surgery
Date c.1000–1350 Height of Church influence on medicine — Galen’s works taught in Church universities
Stat ~90% Medieval European hospitals were Church-run — religion shaped all medical care
Term Church authority The Church backed Galen’s ideas as consistent with Christian thinking — challenged = heresy
Term Dissection ban Church restricted human dissection — slowed anatomical knowledge
Term Prayer as medicine The Church taught illness was God’s punishment — prayer and pilgrimage were treatments
Term Pilgrimage Journey to holy sites for healing — part of the Church’s approach to medicine
Person Medieval Church Controlled universities and hospitals — both helped (care of the sick) and hindered (blocked new ideas) medicine
Person Thomas Aquinas 13th C — reconciled Christian faith with classical learning; kept Galen’s ideas intellectually respectable

Think like a historian

  • Can the same institution be both the most important provider of healthcare and the biggest obstacle to medical progress?
  • What does this tell us about the difficulty of judging historical institutions as simply “good” or “bad” — and how do we weigh the care they provided against the knowledge they suppressed?

item.title: Medicine in the Islamic World Compared with Europe
item.description:
What happened & why it matters

  • Translation movement (8th–9th C)
    • At the time — Islamic scholars preserved and extended Greek texts
    • Long term — these texts returned to Europe and helped spark the Renaissance
  • Canon of Medicine (1025)
    • At the time — the most advanced medical textbook
    • Long term — used in European universities until the 17th century

Key knowledge — DSTEP

Type Item Why it matters
Date c.800–1200 AD Islamic Golden Age of medicine — while Europe stagnated, Islamic scholars advanced
Date c.900s Al-Razi writing — identified measles and smallpox as separate diseases
Date c.1025 Avicenna’s Canon of Medicine published — the most comprehensive medical textbook of the medieval world
Stat 5 volumes Avicenna’s Canon of Medicine — covered all known medicine; used in European universities for 600 years
Term Islamic Golden Age c.800–1200 AD — Islamic scholars translated, preserved and extended Greek medical texts
Term Canon of Medicine Ibn Sina (Avicenna) c.1025 — encyclopaedic medical text; adopted by European universities
Term Bimaristan Islamic hospital — more advanced than European equivalents; separate wards for different diseases
Term Al-Razi (Rhazes) Identified measles and smallpox as distinct diseases — practical clinical observation
Person Ibn Sina (Avicenna) c.980–1037 — Canon of Medicine; the most important Islamic medical scholar

  • What does it tell us about the history of knowledge that the most advanced medicine in the medieval world was happening in Baghdad and Cairo rather than Paris or Oxford?
  • What does the Islamic world’s role in transmitting Greek texts back to Europe during the Renaissance tell us about how knowledge is never lost forever — just displaced?

What happened & why it matters

    • At the time — banned clergy from surgery

item.title: Black Death (1348-49)
item.description:
What happened & why it matters

  • Black Death in England (1348)
    • At the time — medicine completely powerless
    • Long term — exposed the total failure of humour theory; may have stimulated questioning of authority
  • Flagellant movement
    • At the time — religious response to pestilence
    • Long term — shows how far medicine failed; people turned to religion

Key knowledge — DSTEP

Type Item Why it matters
Date 1347 Black Death arrives in Sicily from Asia — spreads rapidly through Europe
Date 1348–49 Peak in England — kills roughly 1/3 of the population
Date 1350s onwards Returns repeatedly — medieval Europe never fully recovered demographically
Stat 1/3 Proportion of England’s population killed — approximately 1.5–2 million people
Stat 25 million Deaths across Europe from the Black Death
Stat Up to 60% Death rates in some English towns — shows the total failure of medical response
Term Black Death Bubonic plague caused by Yersinia pestis — spread by fleas on rats
Term Miasma theory Dominant explanation — bad air causes disease; explains ineffective responses
Term Flagellants People who whipped themselves to appease God — shows the religious response to disease
Term Quarantine Isolation of the sick — one of the few partially effective responses
Person Medieval physicians Helpless — prescribed herbs, bloodletting, prayer; nothing worked
Person Edward III King during the Black Death — government response was ineffective; attempted some quarantine measures

Think like a historian

  • What might the catastrophic failure of Galenic medicine in 1348 have planted in people’s minds about the old certainties?
  • What does the Black Death tell us about the gap between medical theory and medical practice — and about what happens when a theory is not just wrong but actively leads to harmful treatment?
  • Might the scale of the failure have been the first crack in people’s confidence in the Galenic system — a slow seed of doubt that eventually helped fuel the Renaissance?

What happened & why it matters

    • At the time — revolutionary spread of knowledge

    • At the time — Greek scholars fled to Western Europe

Date 1543 Vesalius publishes — the clearest single example of change beginning

Stat 200+ Errors in Galen corrected by Vesalius — enabled by human dissection, not animal

What happened & why it matters

  • Publication of De Humani Corporis Fabrica (1543)

Type Item Why it matters

item.title: Paré
item.description:
What happened & why it matters

  • Battle of Villane (1536)
    • At the time — accidental discovery that gentler wound treatment worked better
    • Long term — began to replace cauterisation; an example of chance leading to progress
  • Paré publishes (1545, 1561)
    • At the time — shared new surgical methods
    • Long term — printing press enabled his ideas to reach other surgeons

Type Item Why it matters

Date 1545 Paré publishes his Method of Treating Wounds — sharing his discoveries
Date 1561 Paré publishes work on surgery including use of ligatures
Stat 3 Paré’s egg yolk, rose oil and turpentine mixture components — replaced boiling oil
Term Ligature Tying off blood vessels instead of cauterisation — Paré’s key surgical innovation
Term Cauterisation Burning wounds with hot iron or boiling oil — the standard (painful, shocking) practice before Paré
Term Battlefield surgery Context of Paré’s discoveries — war drove practical innovation
Term Prosthetics Paré also designed artificial limbs — shows breadth of his contribution
Person Ambroise Paré 1510–90 — French battlefield surgeon; replaced boiling oil with egg yolk mixture; used ligatures; designed prosthetics
Person Vesalius Contemporary — both show how Renaissance observation over authority transformed medicine

  • What does Paré’s story tell us about the role of necessity and chance in medical progress?
  • Why is it significant that the discovery came from a battlefield surgeon with no formal university education — rather than from a learned physician trained in Galen — and what does that tell us about whose knowledge was valued in this period?

item.description:
What happened & why it matters

  • Publication of De Motu Cordis (1628)
    • At the time — overturned Galen’s blood theory
    • Long term — demonstrated the power of experiment; directly contradicted the Church-endorsed Galen

Type Item Why it matters
Date 1578 Harvey born — trained at Padua (Italy), the leading anatomy university
Date 1628 De Motu Cordis published — proved blood circulates continuously

item.title: Edward Jenner and Vaccination (1796)
item.description:
What happened & why it matters

  • Jenner vaccinates James Phipps (1796)
    • At the time — first vaccine; tested on a child (ethically problematic by today’s standards)
    • Long term — eradicated smallpox; founded the principle of vaccination
  • Government funds vaccination (1840)
    • At the time — first government-funded medical intervention
    • Long term — established the principle of state involvement in public health

Key knowledge — DSTEP

Type Item Why it matters
Date 1796 Jenner tests cowpox vaccine on James Phipps — the first vaccination
Date 1798 Jenner publishes his findings — vaccination goes public
Date 1840 Vaccination made free by British government
Date 1853 Vaccination made compulsory in Britain
Date 1980 WHO declares smallpox eradicated — Jenner’s vaccine achieved this
Stat ~400,000 Europeans dying from smallpox each year before Jenner
Stat 1980 Year smallpox was officially eradicated — the only human disease fully eliminated
Term Vaccination Using a weakened or related disease to create immunity — Jenner’s term (from vacca, cow)
Term Cowpox Mild disease in dairy maids — Jenner noticed they didn’t catch smallpox
